cards.title: Gemini 4 Neon is the new #1 on the Models Engineering Index

depth.text: a new index puts **Google's Neon** at the top of its **engineering rankings**

The Models Engineering Index gives 4 Neon a **68.1** score from a composite across **ten coding benchmarks**, adjusted for difficulty and missing results. The page warns that models were tested on **different subsets** and that benchmarks are only a proxy for real engineering work.

cards.camps: Two camps: some users say Neon performs well in real coding work; critics question the index because Neon appears in only 3 of 8 benchmarks.

depth.text: the post calls paid advertising a **98% slot machine** and an **extraction tax**

cards.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)

depth.text: a **base64 encoding bug** could make a program write past the end of a **buffer**

The latest patch uses **OPENSSL_assert()** for inputs that previously caused undefined behavior, while preserving **existing well-defined behavior**. It also applies the fix to EVP_DecodeBlock() and corrects base64encode()'s length check; reviewers debated whether **returning -1** could break callers.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say this could be exploitable if untrusted, very large input reaches it; others say the required input is so huge that CVSS 9.8 is exaggerated.

comments.text: On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB. EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64. https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/ As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the…

I think CVSS 9.8 is exaggerated. This is not remotely anywhere near as serious as Heartbleed. It's an internal function which will fail if its input is far too long, but exploitability rests on how untrusted input can reach it; the key word being "untrusted". E.g. if you operate a base64 encoding service on the Internet that just reads all the data into memory at once and calls EVP_EncodeBlock()…

I am not a system administrator, but I am getting a serious vulnerability fatigue, every single day there's at least two new vulnerabilities in major pieces of software, I'm just tired of seeing that everywhere and hearing that everywhere. Fellow system administrators must be having it much worse.

The more I see these posts, the more I'm convinced that "never reinvent the wheel" mentality we had so far in software engineering basically covered up a lot of lazy engineering, and we just pretended everything was fine. It's like these findings cross-pollinate.

:/
I really need a day off from patching servers.

cards.title: Unblockable communication with gravity

depth.text: someone looked at sending messages with gravity, and commenters are arguing whether it’s truly **unblockable**

The quoted setup uses a mass and an **off-the-shelf, hand-held gravimeter**; a commenter cites a change of **∼5 nm/s^2**, and another points to **1 bit per minute**. Others say flooding the environment with noise could block the signal.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter argues mass cannot be screened; skeptics say noise can jam the signal or nearby devices can fake a receiver’s reading.

comments.text: Would it be easy to jam the signal ? Say, you have a big, heavy double pendulum moving close to the emitter. The moving mass would disturb the signal, and predicting the evolution of a double pendulum is not easy due to its instability (it's not periodic for example, so no Fourier analysis)

It seems like they missed the opportunity to put the big heavy thing on a rotating disk and then encode the data as changes in velocity (frequency domain) which is way easier to do than an elevator, especially with a PM motor. This is basically FM vs AM. Intuitively if the thing is heavy enough it should have decent range, for example humans can “feel” an object of 100 tons spinning at decent…

The key idea seems to be: Since mass cannot be negative, there is no gravitational analog of charge cancelation and hence no way to hide or screen the presence of mass. Perhaps they address this in the paper, but it occurs to me that the obvious countermeasure is to shield with a large positive mass, and then to selectively remove some of this mass to cancel the attempted message.

I think this idea was long time known to astronomers, which in addition to electromagnetic waves use gravitational waves and neutrinos as the media to transmit information. Something other than those three would be novel, I assume.
With an array of gravimeters, you could probably build an unblockable position tracker too.

cards.title: Cooling buildings is overtaking heating them as an energy need, IEA says

depth.text: cooling is **overtaking heating** as an **energy need** in buildings, the IEA says

comments.text: This is an ok development in my opinion because cooling buildings with heat pumps or AC overlaps the demand curve with the solar production curve better than heating does. Heating tends to be during shorter days and less solar production, making it trickier to cover the power needs with new energy alone. Of course this doesn’t mean heating is going down, just that cooling is going up (unless…

What's this headline mean? That everywhere is warmer now so we need more cooling? (Implies global warming) That developing countries need more cooling than heat? (Buried lead) That datacenters make up the majority of new demand ? (Misleading headline) I see many comments here assuming it means continuous energy needs. From the article, we see the headline implies my second question: > That growth…

The great news is that its usually only hot when the suns out, and AC units can be run from solar panels essentially for free. So we can sit in our air conditioned rooms without having to feel guilty for killing the planet.

In the US it's distribution seems to be handled by Nu-Calgon and for whatever reason they branded it…

glossary.composite index: A score made by combining several results into one number.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.error bars: Marks on a chart that show how uncertain a measurement may be.
glossary.OEM: Original Equipment Manufacturer: the company responsible for a laptop’s design and how its parts work together.
glossary.bootloader unlocking: A way to let a phone start a different operating system from the one it came with.
glossary.antitrust: Rules meant to stop companies from becoming so powerful that they can squeeze out competition.
glossary.ad auction: A process where advertisers compete to have their ads shown.
glossary.ROI: Return on investment: a way to ask whether what something achieves is worth what it costs.
glossary.ROAS: Return on ad spend: a way to compare money earned from ads with the money spent on them.
glossary.COGS: Cost of goods sold: what it costs a business to make or buy the products it sells.
glossary.whales: A small number of customers who spend a lot of money in a game.
glossary.aggregator: A tool or site that gathers items from different places into one place.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.ad network: A service that helps websites show ads from advertisers.
glossary.self-hosting: Running a model on computers you control instead of using someone else's online service.
glossary.moderation: Deciding which posts or comments stay up and handling rule-breaking.
glossary.base64: A way to rewrite data using a limited set of characters so it can be carried in places that expect text; it is not encryption.
glossary.buffer overflow: When a program reads or writes beyond the space set aside for data.
glossary.undefined behavior: A situation where C++ gives no guarantee about what the program will do.
glossary.OPENSSL_assert(): A check that stops execution if a condition the code expects turns out to be false.
glossary.CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a scale people use to rate how serious a security flaw is.
glossary.ransomware gang: Criminals who use software to lock or threaten to release data to pressure someone for payment.
glossary.third-party vendor: A separate company hired to provide a service, rather than the company whose customers' data is involved.
glossary.CCPA: California Consumer Privacy Act: a California law that gives people rights over how businesses use their personal information.
glossary.GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation: a European law that sets rules for how organizations use people's personal information.
glossary.two-factor authentication: A sign-in check that asks for a second proof, such as a code, after your password.
glossary.gravimeter: A tool that measures how strong gravity is at a particular spot.
glossary.Faraday cage: A metal enclosure that blocks radio signals from reaching what's inside.
glossary.Fourier analysis: A way to describe a changing signal by breaking it into simpler repeating patterns.
glossary.IEA: International Energy Agency: a group of countries that coordinates work on energy issues.
glossary.TWh: Terawatt-hour: a way to count a huge amount of electricity produced or used.
glossary.peak demand: The most electricity a power grid has to supply at one time during the year.
glossary.useful energy: The energy that does the job people want, such as the heat produced by a heater.
